_comment: SEAT OWNERSHIP BOUNDARY — one source of truth, read by both sides.
TicketForge is one product booted as one system against ONE database. Two
families write to the same seat inventory and neither owns it:
* the interactive (browser) suites under conformance/ hold,
release and buy NAMED seats, because a browser suite that grabs 'the
first available seat' is order-dependent and flaky;
* the analytics fixture (contract/analytics/fixture.sql) SELLS named seats,
because the data family is graded on an exact transaction history.
Until this file existed the two sets overlapped and 7 of 14 e2e tests failed
on an integrated run: the fixture had already sold the seat the browser was
about to hold. The boundary below makes that collision a build failure
instead of a mystery.
THE RULE
Within every event and every section, the seat rows listed in
`interactive_rows` belong to the interactive suites. The analytics fixture
MUST NOT touch a seat in those rows: no hold, no order, no status change.
Every other row (03 and up in every section of every event) is analytics
territory.
WHY ROWS
Seat price is a function of (event, section) only, so the fixture can be
moved to a higher row within the same section and every money answer in
contract/analytics/questions.yaml is unchanged. Rows are also how the seed
is laid out, so the boundary reads off a seat id without a lookup table:
seat_arena_B01-01 is row 01 -> interactive; seat_arena_B03-01 -> analytics.
SECOND BOUNDARY: WHERE A HELD SEAT MAY SIT
Rows are not the whole story. conformance/e2e's availability-filter test
holds one seat and then asserts how many held seats a whole arena section
contains (web.spec.ts: filter-section + filter-availability held ->
toHaveCount). That is a count over an entire section, so no row boundary
can satisfy it: any `active` hold the analytics fixture leaves in the same
section breaks it, whatever row it is in.
So the fixture parks its still-running holds in one declared section per
event -- `analytics_hold_sections` below -- and make-fixture.py fails if a
seat it leaves `held` sits anywhere else. An active hold carries no order,
so its section is not an input to any answer in questions.yaml; moving one
is free. Sold seats are not restricted: no suite counts those.
This half cannot be grepped out of the specs the way named seat ids can: a
section letter and an expected count are ordinary-looking test literals,
invisible from the fixture side. So the TEST side reads this file too.
Every browser suite's helpers.ts (conformance/e2e/helpers.ts among them) exposes
expectedHeldSeatCount(event_id, section, seats_this_test_holds)
which derives the expected number from `analytics_hold_sections` below plus
the test's own holds, and FAILS with the reason if a test tries to count in
the fixture's own section (or holds a seat outside `interactive_rows`).
Every held-seat count in the browser suites goes through it.
So: if you add an interactive test that counts held (or not-available)
seats in a section, get the number from expectedHeldSeatCount() rather than
writing it down. Moving an entry below then breaks that test loudly instead
of silently changing what its count means, and both halves of this boundary
are enforced by machine -- each from the side that can see the claim.
HOW IT IS ENFORCED
contract/analytics/make-fixture.py reads this file, greps every seat id out
of the spec files under the directories in `owners` — and of any other
directory under conformance/ that holds browser specs — and refuses to write
fixture.sql if either side has crossed the line:
- a fixture seat in an interactive row, or in any id a spec names;
- a spec seat OUTSIDE the interactive rows (a new e2e test that reaches
into analytics territory is just as much a collision);
- a spec file that yields no seat ids at all, which would mean the grep
has stopped seeing the suite and the check has quietly gone blind.
Widening the boundary is therefore a deliberate edit here plus a fixture
regeneration, never an accident.
NOT COVERED BY THIS FILE
conformance/api and the web happy-path test deliberately take 'the first
available seat' of event_arena_2000. The seats endpoint orders by section,
row, number, so those picks always land in section A — which is why no
interactive test names a section A arena seat it needs to be AVAILABLE,
and why the analytics fixture may not be graded on a database the API
suite has run against (it would add orders). See the sequencing note in
contract/analytics/README.md.
